stem_history: The lexical strī is subordinate in ati + strī. Its final long vowel shortens in this compound under 1.2.48 with the feminine suffix history. The three genders of the whole compound govern its outer case endings.

policies.decision: iyaṅ survives, producing atistriyau or atistriyoḥ. The Kaumudī’s verse names both suffix environments.

policies.scope: masculine and feminine, am or śas
policies.decision: iyaṅ is optional. The contracted accusative singular ends in short -im after compound shortening. The contracted accusative plural has -īn in the masculine and -īḥ in the feminine.

policies.scope: masculine and feminine jas, including plural address
policies.decision: 7.3.109 supplies guṇa e; 6.1.78 gives ay before the vowel. The Bālamanoramā expressly says guṇa blocks iyaṅ. The masculine nominative and vocative plural are therefore atistrayaḥ. The ordinary feminine here follows the masculine by the Kaumudī. The archive reads atistriyaḥ in all four.

policies.scope: masculine instrumental singular and single-number obliques
policies.decision: the later nā/guṇa/au operations block iyaṅ in their domains, giving atistriṇā, atistraye, atistreḥ, atistrau. The genitive plural takes nuṭ and retroflexion in atistrīṇām.
the short-i stem admits the optional nadī treatment in the relevant ṅ-marked cases and the two schedules recorded in the table. For example, the dative singular is atistraye or atistriyai.

num prevails in the direct dual and plural, atistriṇī and atistrīṇi. Pāṇini 7.1.74 permits the masculine treatment in the stated obliques in Gālava’s usage. The dative includes atistriṇe and atistraye.

source_distinctions.Kaumudi_prose: The digitized masculine nominative line has atistriyaḥ immediately after jasi ca and later prints he atistrayaḥ. Its subsequent verse restricts iyaṅ to the specified environments.
source_distinctions.Balamanorama: Its explicit guṇa and ay account for atistrayaḥ; the same text spells out atistriyoḥ in the dual, where the archive agrees.
